nodes.label: Jonathan Israel
nodes.description: A historian of the Dutch Republic, European Jewry and the Enlightenment whose radical-Enlightenment interpretation gives philosophical ideas a strong explanatory role. In a 2023 interview, Israel argues that the reception of Spinoza helped create a radical current committed to secularism, democratic republicanism and freedom of expression, which he opposes to a moderate Enlightenment. The coherence and reach of that current are disputed. Antoine Lilti stresses the diversity of the most heterodox Enlightenment writings and the ambiguity of ‘Spinozism’ as a historian’s category. David Bell credits Israel’s range and his insistence on ideas, but argues that he infers influence from similarity, takes passages out of context and overstates the ideological causes of the French Revolution.

nodes.label: Geoffrey Parker
nodes.description: A historian of early modern Europe, war and the Spanish monarchy whose work connects military organization with the resources and reach of states. The Army of Flanders and the Spanish Road (1972) began as a Cambridge doctorate under John Elliott, from Elliott’s question of how Spain sustained its army in the Netherlands. The Military Revolution (1988) extended Michael Roberts’s thesis to fortification and the scale of armies, and made it an argument about the rise of the West; it has remained a debate rather than a settled explanation. Global Crisis (2013) connects the political upheavals of the seventeenth century with climatic change across regions.

nodes.label: T. M. Devine
nodes.description: A historian of Scottish society, economy and diaspora. The Tobacco Lords (1975) studied Glasgow’s tobacco merchants, Clanship to Crofters’ War (1994) the social transformation of the Highlands, and The Scottish Nation (1999) is his history of modern Scotland. In ‘Did Slavery Make Scotia Great?’ (2011) he reopens Eric Williams’s question about slavery and economic development, arguing that Scotland’s stake cannot be measured by the few slaving voyages from its ports but must include the wider plantation economies. With Jenny Wormald he called for comparative, internationalized Scottish history rather than an insular national narrative.

nodes.label: Richard J. Evans
nodes.description: A historian of modern Germany who has also defended historical knowledge in public. In Defence of History (1997) answers the writers who brought postmodernist epistemology into historical theory; he names Hayden White, Frank Ankersmit, Keith Jenkins, Patrick Joyce, Dominick LaCapra and Beverley Southgate. He wrote it because the standard textbooks were still Carr’s What Is History? and Elton’s The Practice of History, which he found inadequate. Its introduction accepts White’s point that historians can learn from outside scrutiny of how historical knowledge is made, while rejecting Joyce’s claim that historians must accept postmodernity as an inescapable condition. Death in Hamburg (1987) connects cholera with social inequality and civic government. He served as an expert witness on the falsification of history in the 2000 Irving libel trial, and The Coming of the Third Reich (2003) began his history of Nazi Germany.

nodes.label: Thomas W. Laqueur
nodes.description: A cultural historian of the body, sexuality and death. Making Sex (1990) argues that a ‘one-sex’ model, in which men and women were thought to share the same basic body, gave way in the eighteenth century to a ‘two-sex’ model grounded in biological difference: sex difference itself has a history. The thesis has been both influential and contested. Brooke Holmes, drawing on work by Katharine Park, Robert Nye, Joan Cadden and Helen King, argues that the evidence shows more varied and coexisting models, and traces the book’s narrative of epochal rupture to Foucault’s history of sexuality. Caroline Walker Bynum drew on it while noting Park and Nye’s qualification. Solitary Sex (2003) is a cultural history of masturbation, and The Work of the Dead (2015) asks what the care and naming of the dead do for the living.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Making Sex (1990); Solitary Sex (2003); The Work of the Dead (2015).

nodes.label: Charles S. Maier
nodes.description: A historian of modern Europe and of political organization. His first book, Recasting Bourgeois Europe (1975), compares France, Germany and Italy after the First World War and argues that they did not return to the prewar order but achieved a new balance between state authority and organized interests. The Unmasterable Past (1988) addressed history, the Holocaust and German national identity. In later work he treats territoriality as a historical resource: borders, sovereignty and technologies of communication shape both government and belonging, and a networked world has not abolished the state. A conference report records John Breuilly’s challenge to the coherence of an ‘age of territoriality’, and Partha Chatterjee’s contrast with the overlapping sovereignties of Mughal India and the flexible sovereignty of colonial rule.

nodes.label: E. H. Carr
nodes.description: A historian of Soviet Russia and of international relations whose What Is History? (1961) became the standard British introduction to historical method. Carr argued that historians select and give meaning to facts through their questions, so that research and interpretation proceed together; his position was long read as a challenge to objectivist history. G. R. Elton’s The Practice of History (1967) was written in open opposition, and John Tosh called the Carr–Elton controversy the best starting point for debate about the standing of historical knowledge. Richard Evans wrote In Defence of History (1997) because Carr’s and Elton’s books were still the standard textbooks and, in his view, inadequate for later debates. The Twenty Years’ Crisis (1939) belongs to his work on international relations, and his History of Soviet Russia began with The Bolshevik Revolution (1950).

nodes.label: Judith R. Walkowitz
nodes.description: A historian of gender, sexuality and urban life who joins cultural interpretation to material and social conditions. In her Minerva interview, Walkowitz recalls Hayden White’s supervision and his introduction of Foucault as resources for her research. She also identifies E. P. Thompson’s account of lived class formation as opening a route toward gender. Her use of Foucault is selective: she questions his attention to gender and leaves more room for individual and collective agency. The prostitution study examines regulation and feminist alliances; City of Dreadful Delight asks how sexual danger and possibility were narrated across a changing city. Walkowitz cautions that reading only its scandal-centred beginning and ending misses her attempt at a simultaneous, multilayered urban history. The Soho project extends that inquiry to contested cosmopolitan spaces, rather than treating the city as either an uncomplicated refuge or a single landscape of danger.

nodes.label: Paul Kennedy
nodes.description: A historian of international power, strategy and political economy. The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987) argues that great powers decline relative to others when their strategic commitments outrun their economic base; readers summarized this as ‘imperial overstretch’, and in the late 1980s it was read as a warning to the United States. Michael Cox notes that the idea was not wholly new, and Kennedy himself traced one stimulus to Mahan’s use of an earlier reflection on Spain’s dispersed empire. In the same roundtable Varsha Venkatasubramanian criticized the book’s neglect of non-state actors and of politics’ effects on economic development; Kennedy accepted her point about India and conceded that the book may contain too much economic determinism. His earlier books studied British naval mastery and the Anglo-German antagonism before 1914.

nodes.label: T. C. Smout
nodes.description: A historian of Scottish society who helped establish environmental history in Scotland. A History of the Scottish People, 1560–1830 (1969) and A Century of the Scottish People (1986) are his social histories of Scotland. His 1990 British Academy lecture ‘The Highlands and the Roots of Green Consciousness’ questions the story that appreciation of Highland landscapes was simply imported into an indifferent society. In later environmental work he draws on E. A. Wrigley’s account of the shift from organic to fossil-fuel economies, and names William Cronon’s city-and-hinterland history as a model for studies of Scottish cities still to be written.
